world_status: statement found in an open source

new_statements.quote: Unlike languages such as English, where stress can be shifted to emphasise the focus constituent, SLs generally favour prominence at the end of phrases and move (contrastive) focus constituent to this position in order to be prosodically marked [...]. [p. 84] || [p. 170] Unlike SLs such as ASL and DGS, where manual prominence is typically conveyed through large articulatory gestures such as wide movements, spatial displacement, repetition, or increased peak velocity [...], the data from LSFB point to a more constrained yet systematic reliance on mouth articulation and duration-based cues, particularly deceleration and manual holds, in marking CF.
new_statements.citation: Lombart, Clara. 2026. In Search of Harmony in Contrast(ive Focus): A Cross-Modal and Cross-Linguistic Analysis of Prosody and Information Structure in French and LSFB. PhD dissertation, Université de Namur / Université de Mons (defended 8 April 2026; supervisors K. Huet and L. Meurant). https://hdl.handle.net/20.500.12907/56014

new_statements.second_reader_evidence: Opened (366 pp., text layer, extracted text). Both halves of the quote are present verbatim at the stated locators: pdf p.107 = printed p.84, sect. 2.1.7 'Remarks on manual prominence' ("Unlike languages such as English, where stress can be shifted to emphasise the focus constituent, SLs generally favour prominence at the end of phrases and move (contrastive) focus constituent to this position in order to be prosodically marked (e.g., Crasborn et al., 2012; Nespor & Sandler, 1999; Wilbur, 1999)"); pdf p.193 = printed p.170, sect. 6.3 ("Unlike SLs such as ASL and DGS, where manual prominence is typically conveyed through large articulatory gestures such as wide movements, spatial displacemen…
new_statements.rule_in_words: LSFB is a signed language; no source gives a position for word (sign-internal) stress, and signs are treated as the syllable-sized unit. Prominence is described as a phrase/discourse-level, information-structure-driven property: contrastively focused signs are made prominent mainly by longer relative duration (deceleration), sign holds and weak-hand holds, and mouth articulations, with eyebrow/head/body-lean cues spanning the focus domain; large movement, spatial displacement and repetition (the ASL/DGS-type cues) play a minor role. Footnote 38 (p. 172) adds that manual prominence is also shaped by movement type, sign type and position in the signed unit, but these lexical/positional factors are not the primary drivers: prominence increases systematically with information structure. Sign languages in general are said to favour prominence at the end of phrases (p. 84, citing Nespor & Sandler 1999, Wilbur 1999, Crasborn et al. 2012).
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not applicable / not discussed. Prominence is scored as gradient (one point per co-occurring manual cue: relative duration >= 1, repetition, dominance reversal, change in vertical location, hold, mouth articulation; p. 109).
new_statements.exceptions: Movement repetition is rare in LSFB (4.8% of all signs, 7.5% of contrastively focused signs; p. 161), unlike RSL/NGT; holds are low-frequency but strongly associated with the 'discourse opposition' subtype of contrast and absent in 'selection' (p. 161). An alternative to repetition is the addition of a movement (p. 161).
new_statements.domain_note: Domain is the signed utterance/phrase in spontaneous and elicited dialogue from the LSFB Corpus (4 native signers in the 2022 case study; larger dataset in the thesis), not citation forms. The statement concerns prosodic prominence encoding contrastive focus, i.e. phrase-level accentuation; it says nothing about a fixed stress position inside a sign. Corroborating first-hand observation from a second saved file: Paligot 2018, p. 140 (pdf 143): 'La deuxième apparition du terme est accentuée : cela se marque par l'ampleur du mouvement, la durée de sa réalisation, et cela a également pour effet de neutraliser l'abaissement' (an accentuated token of the sign COMMENT shows larger movement, longer duration and no lowering), and p. 66 (pdf 69): a prosodic role of internal-movement repetition with more movement cycles at the end of sentences (phrase-final lengthening).
new_statements.identity_note: Sign language (Wallonia/Brussels, Belgium), glottocode lang1248 = ISO sfb. Not to be confused with Flemish Sign Language (VGT, vlaa1235) or LSF (fren1243). Both sources describe LSFB as used by native signers in the LSFB Corpus (UNamur); no dialect split. Positional word stress is not a category any source describes for this language; what is described is prosodic prominence under contrastive focus and phonetic 'accentuated' vs reduced forms of sign tokens.

sources.locator: Ch. 3, sect. 2.1.7 'Remarks on manual prominence', p. 84 (pdf p. 107); Ch. 3, sect. 6 'Discussion and conclusion', p. 170 (pdf p. 193); see also fn. 38, p. 172 (pdf p. 195) and the prominence annotation scheme, p. 109 (pdf p. 132)
sources.note: Ch. 3 reviews manual/non-manual prosodic markers in sign languages and concludes that LSFB marks contrastive-focus prominence mainly by duration cues (deceleration, holds) and mouth articulations rather than by large movements/displacement/repetition (pp. 84, 148-156, 170); prominence is IS-driven, with sign/movement type secondary (fn. 38 p. 172). No word-internal stress position is stated.

sources.note: Phonetic-reduction study (sign lowering, weak drop) by register; no stress rule. p. 140: an 'accentuated' token of a sign shows larger movement, longer duration and neutralised lowering (Fig. 36); p. 66: repetition of sign-internal movement has a prosodic role, with more cycles at the end of sentences (phrase-final lengthening); accentuation flagged as an uncontrolled factor for future work (pp. 140, 243).
